claims.text: The initial refractory high-entropy alloy lacks significant aluminum content.
The initial alloy has poor oxygen resistance at extreme temperatures.
The intervention is to add 5–10 wt% aluminum to the alloy.
Adding 5–10 wt% aluminum will promote formation of a continuous alumina scale during high-temperature exposure.
The alumina scale formed after aluminum addition will be adherent.
At elevated temperature, added aluminum will diffuse to the alloy surface.
Surface-enriched aluminum will oxidize to form an Al2O3 layer.
The Al2O3 layer will act as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
Reduced oxygen ingress will suppress further oxidation of the underlying alloy.
The aluminum-modified alloy will have lower oxidation weight gain than the untreated alloy.
The aluminum-modified alloy will exhibit a well-formed, continuous alumina scale.
Under the same exposure conditions, the untreated alloy will have a higher oxidation rate than the aluminum-modified alloy.
Under the same exposure conditions, the untreated alloy will form a less protective oxide than the aluminum-modified alloy.
The predicted benefit is intended to occur at approximately 1100 °C in ambient air for exposures up to 100 hours.
The oxidation-resistance benefit may not persist at substantially different temperatures or oxygen partial pressures.
Failure to obtain both a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain and a continuous protective alumina scale relative to the untreated alloy will falsify the hypothesis.
